summary: A report on an experiment linking two math systems over the ARPANET: MIT's MATHLAB, strong at symbolic manipulation, and UCSB's OLS, strong at interactive numeric work. It was an example of resource sharing using Telnet and remote job service, with numbers sent as character text.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 525 describes a link between two systems with different math capabilities. Users could prepare symbolic expressions at MIT and transfer them to UCSB for numerical evaluation and plotting.

questions: how did mathlab connect to ucsb ols
subtitle: An experiment that moved mathematical expressions from MIT MATHLAB to UCSB OLS.

tldr.problem: MIT's MATHLAB and UCSB's OLS supported different kinds of mathematics, so users had to translate results by hand to use both systems.
tldr.mechanism: The experiment saved selected MATHLAB expressions, transferred them through a batch job, translated them into OLS programs, and stored them at UCSB for numeric work and plotting.
tldr.outcome: The report documents a working resource-sharing experiment, limited to real expressions and dependent on the systems and network functioning.

today: The unit records RFC 525's status as Unknown and lists no updates or obsoleting RFCs. It documents an experiment in sharing resources between MIT MATHLAB and UCSB OLS.

sections.title: Combining Two Kinds of Mathematics
sections.content:
MATHLAB at MIT offered symbolic manipulation through MACSYMA. UCSB's OLS supported interactive numeric and graphics work. Before the experiment, users who wanted both kinds of work had to translate information between the systems by hand.

The experiment aimed to provide an automated path from expressions in MATHLAB to user programs at UCSB. The documented implementation was limited to evaluating real functions.
sections.plainLanguage: MATHLAB could work with mathematical symbols, while OLS could calculate with numbers and draw plots. The experiment connected them so users could use both capabilities.

sections.title: Transferring Expressions to OLS
sections.content:
The user connects to MATHLAB, performs symbolic work and marks the expression lines to retrieve. A SAVE function writes the selected lines to a file. The user then connects to OLS and runs programs that ask for the source and destination files and submit a batch job.

A program at UCSB retrieves the expressions, translates them into OLS form and stores them in an OLS user directory. The user can load the returned programs, set values for variables and display or plot the results. The report's example shows this sequence using expressions and their derivatives and integrals.
sections.plainLanguage: The user marks expressions at MIT and saves them in a file. A UCSB batch job retrieves and translates them, after which OLS can evaluate or plot the results.

sections.title: Limits and Possible Additions
sections.content:
The current program transfers expressions, but not equations or functions. It recognizes only one-letter variable names and does not handle complex numbers. The transfer also depends on the UCSB computer, the network and the MIT PDP-10, and software changes at either site can cause difficulties.

The authors list possible additions, including complex-number recognition, more translation rules and tools for setting up numerical sweeps and plots. They also describe a possible extension that would turn a MATHLAB function into an OLS program.
sections.plainLanguage: The experiment has limits: it handles only certain real expressions and one-letter variable names. The authors describe several possible improvements, but do not say they were implemented.
